title: The Dangerous Addiction to Miracle Stories
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Salinas argues that leaders and creators are drawn to miracle stories of overnight success, and that this teaches the wrong lesson: that audacious risk beats patient strategy. He names survivorship bias as the mechanism, since the many who made the same bold move and failed are invisible. He adds a second distortion, taking credit for wins as brilliance while blaming failures on the market, which shuts off honest reflection and breeds overconfidence. Against this he sets a long-game view in which greatness is slow, repetitive and unglamorous. The practical prescription is small bets, knowing what you can afford to lose, separating ego from outcomes, and celebrating consistency, supported by scripture-based epigraphs.
points: Survivorship bias makes success look like a product of gutsiness alone, hiding the larger set of people who tried the same moves and failed.
Treating wins as genius and losses as bad luck protects the ego but kills growth, so honest post-mortems are a leadership discipline.
Overconfidence after a few wins makes decision-makers reckless, in leadership as in writing.
Apparent overnight successes were usually compounding skills and relationships for years before anyone noticed.
The recommended habits are small bets, knowing your risk profile and celebrating consistency over flash.
quotes: But there’s a quiet danger behind this obsession: it teaches the wrong lesson, that success is about audacious risk-taking, not patient strategy or disciplined execution. We end up glorifying risk for its own sake, forgetting that for every miracle story we hear, there are a thousand silent failures we don’t.

This is survivorship bias, the human tendency to notice only the winners and ignore the losers. It creates a distorted view of reality, making success look like a function of gutsiness alone, rather than what it really is: a delicate mix of timing, preparation, iteration, and yes, a sprinkle of luck.
If you model your life and business on these outlier stories, you’re not leading — you’re gambling. And gamblers don’t build legacies.
It’s a comforting story. It protects our ego. But it kills our growth. True leadership, true craftsmanship, and true business acumen come from honest reflection.

In leadership, overconfidence after a few wins can make decision-makers reckless. In writing, a sudden viral moment can make you think you’ve cracked the code, when often it was just the right topic at the right time.
Chasing unicorns is fun to fantasize about. But building a life, a career, or a movement isn’t about jackpot moments. It’s about bricks.
